audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict penultimate, domain word, rule 10/010/0010..) rests on a held, full reference grammar of exactly this languoid (van Klinken 1999, PL C-155), and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated place (sec. 2.3.3, pp.18-19). Her analysis supports 'strict': she calls the penultimate rule 'exceptionless' once long vowels are analysed as disyllabic geminates, and the only antepenultimate surface forms involve the extrametrical enclitic -kan, i.e. outside the stress domain as coded. sources.quote: p.311: 'In native words, stress is always on the penultimate syllable (most of the lexical words have two to four syllables): hemu [ˈhe.mu], hamutuk [ha.ˈmu.tuk]. However, in borrowings, stress can fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. Portuguese loanwords keep their original stress...' p.134: 'Since the stress in Tetun Prasa is fixed on the penultimate syllable, speakers with little knowledge of Portuguese encounter problems pronouncing Portuguese borrowings that kept their original stress pattern (Albuquerque 2011:92).' NOTE: this describes Tetun Prasa (= Tetun Dili, te
sources.locator: sec. 7.5.1 'Stress and syllable structure', printed p.311 (PDF p.316); also p.134 (PDF p.139) summarising Albuquerque 2011:92
sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked 'grammar' (520 pp) for tetu1245; downloaded and read - confirms fixed penultimate stress for native vocabulary but concerns Tetun Prasa, so it adds corroboration only.
